summary:
Amapá's own legal layer sits on top of the national framework. Law No. 1,417/2009 provides administrative sanctions for discrimination motivated by gender identity or sexual orientation within the state public service. State Law No. 2,790/2022 makes discrimination on those grounds a crime, and Ordinary Law No. 2,710/2022 typifies anti-LGBTQ discrimination at state sports venues, football stadiums included, as an administrative offence. State Law No. 1,680/2012 established the State Day to Combat Homophobia, observed each 27 May.

Two state bodies carry the protection machinery: the State Council for Combating Discrimination and CELGBT, which run awareness campaigns and issue public repudiations of discriminatory acts against the LGBTQIAPN+ population. The source inventory contains no state-level enforcement statistics or case outcomes for these laws, so how they operate in practice cannot be assessed from the material available.

Civil-registry rectification is handled locally. On 19 February 2022 the Public Defender's Office of Amapá filed the state's first request for name and gender rectification on behalf of a non-binary person, treating the request as legally viable on the same self-determination basis as for transgender people and arguing that the registry should reflect social presentation. The procedure follows the ordinary civil-registry alteration process, and the Defender's Office assists applicants. Since 2022 the office has made legal gender change accessible to non-binary people in the state.

Gender-affirming care is available through the public system. On 13 February 2025 the Macapá municipal government opened the state's first Municipal Trans Outpatient Clinic, at the Papaléo Paes Specialties Center, running Monday to Friday from 08:00 to 17:00. It offers free multidisciplinary transition care to trans, travesti and non-binary people with no age restriction: general medicine, nursing, endocrinology, gynecology, dermatology, psychiatry, urology, cardiology, psychology, nutrition, social work, physiotherapy, speech therapy, dentistry, laboratory tests, ultrasound, mammography, densitometry, vaccination, rapid tests, Pap smear collection and dressings, with testosterone cypionate and estradiol supplied under clinical protocol. Entry is by referral from a basic health unit or by walking in; the first appointment is a general-practitioner evaluation with onward referral, and clinical demands unrelated to gender transition are excluded. Statewide gender-affirming services also run through the University Hospital of the Federal University of Amapá and the AMA-LBTI Center, which serves lesbian, bisexual, travesti, transsexual and intersex women.

Family formation has drawn judicial attention. In mid-2025 the Court of Justice of Amapá ran the campaign "Every form of love can also be family" under CNJ Resolution No. 532/2023, aimed at ensuring transgender people face no discrimination during the adoption qualification process. Adoption by same-sex couples has been recognised in the state since the national 2010 ruling; a couple from Santana obtained an adoption in 2016 after six years of proceedings, and in 2017 the Legislative Assembly considered a bill extending maternity or paternity leave to same-sex adoptive couples on the same terms as heterosexual families.
tangentialFactors: Marriage equality reached Amapá through the National Council of Justice resolution of 2013 rather than through any state act. The state had no formal recognition of same-sex unions before that date, although stable unions existed in Amapá according to national statistics agency data.
localsOnly:
Residents reach the Municipal Trans Outpatient Clinic in Macapá by referral from a basic health unit or by walking in. Intake requires an RG identity card, a CPF tax number and a SUS card. The clinic operates Monday to Friday, 08:00 to 17:00, and does not treat clinical demands unrelated to gender transition.

The Public Defender's Office of Amapá assists with civil-registry name and gender rectification, which follows the same procedure as any other civil-registry alteration.

State Law No. 1,417/2009 exposes discrimination by gender identity or sexual orientation within the state public service to administrative sanctions, and the State Council for Combating Discrimination and CELGBT handle awareness work and public repudiation of discriminatory acts.
outOfScopeNotes:
The 2017 Legislative Assembly bill on leave for same-sex adoptive couples is recorded as a bill; whether it was enacted is not established in the sources.

No Amapá-specific figures for anti-LGBTQ violence, for prosecutions under State Law No. 2,790/2022, or for administrative proceedings under Ordinary Law No. 2,710/2022 appear in the source inventory, so the practical enforcement of the state's protections is unresolved here.

The state's pre-1830 legal history, including the absence of sodomy provisions from the 1830 Imperial Penal Code and the earlier French-era repeal, is recorded in the sources but bears on no current rule affecting visitors and is not carried into this assessment.
